newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Coffee rally could extend into July - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee rally could extend into July - analysts.

text.p: Arabica coffee futures extended a stunning two-day rally on Thursday and analysts said low inventory levels, combined with the onset of the Brazilian winter, could sustain the bull run for another two months.

"Who is going to short this market going into the (Brazilian) winter with tight supplies?" said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "If Brazil doesn't have a freeze the speculators could go to the bank, but they will probably wait until mid-July."

Worries that cold weather could damage coffee trees in top-producer Brazil typically fuel buying ahead of the country's June through August winter season. Current supply concerns, however, have intensified this year's weather focus, with any signs of cool weather in Brazil likely to spark frenzied buying.
Two severe frosts in June and July, 1994, wiped out Brazil's coffee crop and sent world prices spinning higher.
"Temperatures are becoming cooler and the fact that we're coming into the heart of the cold weather season with the low stock levels makes this rally more sustainable," said one analyst.
Coffee inventories in both consuming and producing countries, currently hovering near 20-year lows, are at the root of the blistering five-month run-up on the futures market.
Futures prices have rocketed more than 150 percent since the beginning of the year, with the CSCE July contract peaking at 318.00 cents a lb on Thursday, a level not seen since 1977.

Supply worries have been exacerbated by forecasts for smaller-than-expected crops in many Latin American countries, labor unrest in the two largest producers, Colombia and Brazil, and projections for a smaller crop in Brazil in the coming 1997/98 season.

Although Brazil is beginning to harvest its new-crop coffee, which does not meet specifications for coffee certified for delivery on the CSCE, analysts said the lack of exchange certifiable mild arabica beans from Central America and Colombia ahead of their harvests this autumn will also underpin the market.

"The perception is that supply is tight and will remain tight into the December contract," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast. "I don't expect to see any enormous amount of coffee coming onto the market between now and October, and that's going to support prices."

But while the market appears to be racing unopposed toward the all-time record futures price of 340.70 cents set on April 14, 1977, some traders feared a consumer backlash in response to higher retail prices.

Large roasters such as Folgers and Maxwell House have already hiked prices on their 13-ounce can of regular ground coffee by nearly 50 percent, and traders said another increase -- the fifth in less than four months -- could be in store for coffee drinkers as soon as next week.
On Wednesday, Starbucks Corp. said it planned to raise prices for the second time this year to reflect the higher cost of coffee beans worldwide.
The Seattle-based retailer and roaster said most coffee beverage prices will increase by $0.05 to $0.10 per cup, while the price of whole beans will increase by $0.40 per pound, effective on Friday.
"It (higher prices) may take some time to affect consumption, but it will eat into it," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "People will try to economize and use less."
